title: Firewall policy interaction matrix — scrapbook and tactical runbook draft
content:
Context:
This is a working notebook / runbook-draft capturing ad hoc experiments, observed interactions, and a tentative mitigation sequence for customer-facing firewall + tenant network-policy collisions that affect control-plane heartbeat reachability in private/VPC deployments. Not a finished postmortem — more of a lab log + operator playbook to be iterated after reruns in lab/testbed and an eventual formal incident review.

Why I wrote this: over the last three customer incidents (INC-2026-06, INC-2026-07, INC-2026-08) we saw a recurring pattern: a combination of DNAT/forwarding rules on customer firewalls + tenant egress/ingress policies leads to asymmetric path selection for control-plane heartbeats. Symptoms often seen: ephemeral control-plane disconnects (~30–120s), occasional TCP RST spikes, followed by a cascade of backpressure on the data path (retransmits + slowdowns).

Top-level hypothesis (working):
- Customer firewall/edge boxes rewrite or pinhole certain ephemeral ports (UDP/TCP) for DNAT to backend appliances.
- Tenant-level policy (kube-netpol or equivalent) enforces egress constraints that are stricter than the firewall expectations.
- When control-plane agents attempt to re-establish sessions, the path chosen by the firewall appliance (based on conntrack state) is sometimes missing the expected source port or NAT pairing, causing either traffic to be dropped or replies to be routed to a different next-hop, which results in TCP RSTs or blackholed UDP heartbeats.

What we observed (lab + customer telemetry snippets):
- 2026-08-12 02:12 UTC: First heartbeat gap detected on customer cluster A. Alert: CP_HEARTBEAT_LOST threshold=45s.
- Packet captures (from customer mirror) show SYN from agent IP X.Y.Z.10 -> control-plane-proxy:443 with source port 42013. Reply arrives with destination port 42012 (off-by-one). Upstream firewall shows DNAT to internal appliance mapping for 42012 only.
- Conntrack table on firewall had two entries for the same tuple but different src-ports; older one evicted earlier causing subsequent replies to end up misrouted.
- Kernel retransmit counters on agent node increased by 4–6 packets in the first 30s.

Quick experiments run in lab (steps + result summary):
1) Recreate DNAT mapping for ephemeral source port range (42000–42100) on the virtual firewall. Result: heartbeat reconnect stable for >15m (test run length).
2) Apply pod egress policy that allows ephemeral high ports to control-plane-proxies; result: no immediate disconnects but slower failure recovery when conntrack evictions forced state mismatch.
3) Force connection reuse (keepalive tweak) to avoid high churn of ephemeral ports. Result: reduced conntrack churn, but customer-side NAT tables still had short timeouts that caused issues under bursty control-plane events.

Operator playbook (tactical steps for on-call) — DRAFT:
Goal: restore control-plane reachability with minimal config changes on customer side, and provide a safe fallback if remediation fails.
Pre-reqs: access to customer firewall management console OR ability to coordinate with customer NIC/ops. SSH access to a control-plane proxy or agent node for tcpdump.

Step 0 — triage (0–5m):
- Confirm alert details (INC ID, affected cluster, start time).
- Pull last 5m agent and control-plane proxy logs.
- Run quick health checks: curl /health on control-plane-proxy, check agent-local metrics (heartbeat_missed_count).
- Start tcpdump on agent and on control-plane-proxy side: tcpdump -nni any 'host <agent-ip> and host <cp-proxy-ip>' and capture for 60s. Save pcap to /tmp and share link with customer.

Step 1 — look for asymmetric ports and DNAT mismatches (5–15m):
- Inspect pcap: are source ports consistent? Is reply destination port matching SYN source port?
- If replies are arriving to different destination port, note the delta (e.g., src:42013 vs dst:42012).
- On customer firewall: ask for conntrack dump or show nat translations (example CLI: show conntrack nat | grep <agent-ip>).

If evidence shows off-by-one or port-rewrite: (15–40m)
- Temporary mitigation A: ask customer to add DNAT entry for the observed dest port (e.g., add mapping for 42012 -> agent) OR broaden DNAT range to include the ephemeral pool (42000–42150).
- Temporary mitigation B: if customer policies disallow DNAT changes, request a short-lived ACL tweak to allow direct egress to control-plane-proxy on destination 443 from agent IPs (bypass DNAT).
- If either mitigation applied, monitor heartbeats for 10 minutes and check for RST spikes.

If no DNAT evidence (packets show proper 1:1 mapping), proceed to Step 2: conntrack eviction pressure (15–45m)
- Check firewall memory and conntrack table sizes. Look for churn.
- Recommend increasing conntrack timeout for TCP_ESTABLISHED or increase table size if safe.
- As alternative, request customer to enable TCP keepalives with longer intervals on our agents (config flag described below) to reduce ephemeral churn.

Step 3 — fallback (45–90m):
- If mitigations fail or customer cannot change firewall, flip group-level routing to an alternate control-plane region (if configured) using the routing policy tool: route policy set --cluster <id> --preferred-region fallback-region.
- If routing flip is not available, escalate to SRE pager for coordinated maintenance window with the customer (may require short restart of control-plane proxy).

Runbook-draft config knobs and notes (for product/infra):
- Agent keepalive defaults: currently 30s/3 probes. Proposed default for private deployments under NAT pressure: 120s/5 probes. Operators should test for side-effects (longer failure detection delays).
- Add control-plane port affinity option: if set, agent will attempt to reuse a pinned source port for the life of the process (config: agent.source_port_affinity=true). Notes: risk of port exhaustion at scale; should be opt-in per-customer.
- Conntrack-friendly NAT range recommendation: advertise ephemeral port pools to customers: 42000-43000 as preferred. Document in onboarding.

Telemetry and alerts to tune (short-term):
- Add a new alert: CP_CONNTRACK_MISMATCH if we detect more than 3 sessions in a 5m window where reply dst-port != orig src-port.
- Plot: agent.retransmit_count, firewall.conntrack_evictions, cp_proxy.tcp_rst_rate — correlate in dashboard.

Open questions (to resolve in formal review):
- How often do customers run stateful firewalls configured with DNAT that will rewrite destination ports in this way? Is our onboarding doc clear about ephemeral port expectations?
- What is acceptable default for keepalive tradeoff between faster failure detection and conntrack churn?
- Can we safely expose a small set of recommended ephemeral source ports at scale without running into global port exhaustion?

Immediate action items (who/when):
- Priya: draft short KB for Support with steps to run tcpdump and identify off-by-one port mismatches (due 2026-08-18).
- Luis: spin up a 3-node testbed with a virtual FW that rewrites DNAT and run longer soak (72h) against the current agent keepalive default, record conntrack evictions (due 2026-08-20).
- Hannah: add a telemetry panel to SRE dashboard that correlates cp heartbeat gaps with conntrack evictions (due 2026-08-19).
- Devon: prototype agent.source_port_affinity toggle and run basic compatibility tests (due 2026-08-24).

Notes for postmortem section (placeholder):
- If lab confirms hypothesis, include a short remediation plan: {{onboarding doc update}}, {{agent config defaults change}}, {{support KB}}, and a list of impacted clusters (if any historical incidents tied to same root cause).
- Consider shipping a lightweight conntrack-diagnostic probe in the agent that can query customer firewall behavior (requires opt-in and explicit permissions).

Appendix — useful commands and snippets:
- tcpdump capture (agent): sudo tcpdump -nni eth0 host <cp-proxy-ip> and host <agent-ip> -w /tmp/agent_cp.pcap
- check agent retransmits (Linux): ss -tan src <agent-ip> | grep retrans | wc -l (approximate)
- sample firewall conntrack dump (vendor CLI varies): show conntrack entries | grep <agent-ip> | grep <cp-proxy-ip>

Slack links and threads: synced to #sre-private (thread: CP heartbeat oscillation) — pinned key pcaps and conntrack screenshots.

Closing note: This doc is intentionally informal — think of it as a lab notebook + operator checklist to reduce time-to-mitigation during noisy customer incidents. Revisions welcome; I expect the lab runs to either confirm DNAT port-rewrite as the primary root cause or push us toward a different transient NAT pathology (e.g., asymmetric return-path via BGP hairpinning).
